title: Exodus in Poilievre's office as 5 staffers plan departures
summary: Sources tell CBC News five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit. The departures will leave big gaps in Poilievre's office,…

image.caption: The departures come as the Conservatives prepare for six byelections in December. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Sources tell CBC News five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit. The departures will leave big gaps in Poilievre's office, particularly in communications and policy.
Directors, senior-level staff informed Opposition leader of plans to leave: sources
Five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit, according to sources.
Those leaving their posts include the deputy chief of staff and director of policy, Aaron Wudrick, who informed caucus last week.
Others include director of communications and issues management, Micah Green, and director of media relations Sam Lilly.
Both are taking new jobs with the newly elected British Columbia Conservative government.
Senior policy adviser Andrew Evans and Poilievre's executive assistant Hayley Quipp have also informed the leader of plans to depart.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to share details about the internal workings of Poilievre's office, but Lilly and Green confirmed their departures in statements.
These departures will leave big gaps in the Opposition leader's office (OLO), particularly in communications and policy.

Wudrick is a longtime Conservative and respected by caucus, previously serving as director of domestic policy at the right-leaning Macdonald-Laurier Institute. Before that, he was the federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation.
He was one of the architects of the party's platform in the 2025 election campaign and has served in OLO for two-and-a-half years.

He was recently promoted to deputy chief of staff. His resignation follows other high-level departures from Poilievre's office earlier this year, including former chief of staff Ian Todd and former director of communications Katy Merrifield.
In an email sent to caucus last week, Wudrick said he would be leaving his role effective Nov. 27 for a job in the private sector in a bid to spend more time with his family.

"It has been an honour and a privilege to serve our leader and this team the last 2.5 years," he wrote, adding that he believes the goal of electing Poilievre to be prime minister "remains achievable in the next election."
Evans has been senior policy adviser since 2024, and previously held roles as a staffer in the Ford government. He was assigned to the immigration file, which has been a focus of the Opposition.
Green and Lilly are Poilievre's office's most senior communications staff. Green replaced Merrifield in April, but has been at OLO in a communications role since December 2022.
His LinkedIn page says he's been working for the Conservatives, either at OLO, the party or through an MP's office, since 2019.

Lilly is a longtime figure on Parliament Hill. He's been in communications with OLO since April 2021, starting as a press secretary and rising to director of media relations. In the 2019 election, he was a candidate for the Conservatives in Edmonton Strathcona.
These departures come as Poilievre faces pressure to keep seats in upcoming byelections after losing nine MPs since the 2025 election.

So far, he has lost four MPs to floor-crossing and four others have either announced plans to resign or have already resigned. Another MP, Quebec's Richard Martel, was appointed to the Senate. He still serves in the Conservative caucus.

items: Carney calls December byelections for 6 ridings in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan

blocks.text: There are six byelections in December.. The Conservatives are incumbents in two: Ontario's Brantford-Brant South and Saskatchewan's Yorkton-Melville.

Both seats were previously considered safe for the Conservatives, but the Carney Liberals' high polling in Ontario could see a fight in Brantford-Brant South, which was vacated by former justice critic Larry Brock.
Brock endorsed a local pastor, Dave Carrol, to succeed him — but the party chose Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis. Carrol later chose to run as an Independent, which risks splitting the Conservative vote.

blocks.text: Online posts and local news reports show Poilievre has been spending time in the riding, including this weekend, in a bid to shore up support.
Conservative sources who have spoken to CBC News in the past say, despite challenging polls, there is no plan to try to remove Poilievre and that he has the support of caucus.
Poilievre sailed through his last leadership review in January with 87.4 per cent of the vote from party members.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.
